nodes.label: Photoelectric and Modern Physics
nodes.note: Modern physics began with the failure of classical waves to explain the photoelectric effect. Einstein's photon picture, $$K_{max} = h\nu - \phi$$, opened quantum theory.

nodes.label: Photoelectric Effect
nodes.note: Light ejects electrons only if each photon carries enough energy. The threshold condition is $$h\nu_0 = \phi$$, where $\phi$ is the work function.

nodes.label: Planck Photon Hypothesis
nodes.note: Light energy is quantized in packets: $$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$, with $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J}\cdot\text{s}$. Higher frequency means more energetic photons, not brighter light.

nodes.label: Photon Energy Example
nodes.note: For $\lambda = 500\ \text{nm}$: $$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \approx 3.98 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} \approx 2.48\ \text{eV}$$.

nodes.label: Einstein Photoelectric Equation
nodes.note: $$K_{max} = h\nu - \phi$$ converts photon energy into electron kinetic energy minus escape cost. It explains threshold frequency and instantaneous emission.

nodes.label: Einstein Equation Example
nodes.note: Light of $\lambda = 400\ \text{nm}$ hits a metal with $\phi = 2.0\ \text{eV}$: photon energy $E \approx 3.1\ \text{eV}$, so $K_{max} \approx 1.1\ \text{eV}$.

nodes.label: Stopping Potential
nodes.note: The reverse voltage that just stops the fastest electrons measures $K_{max}$: $$eV_s = h\nu - \phi$$. A plot of $V_s$ vs $\nu$ is linear with slope $h/e$.

nodes.label: Threshold Frequency and Work Function
nodes.note: Emission starts only above $$\nu_0 = \frac{\phi}{h}$$. Different metals have different $\phi$, so their thresholds differ.

nodes.label: Saturation Current vs Intensity
nodes.note: Saturation photocurrent is proportional to incident intensity (photon flux), while stopping potential is intensity-independent: $$i_{sat} \propto I, \ V_s \text{ independent of } I$$. More photons means more electrons, not faster electrons.

nodes.label: Radiation Pressure
nodes.note: For absorption, pressure is $$P = \frac{I}{c}$$; for perfect reflection, $$P = \frac{2I}{c}$$. Momentum transfer per photon is $p = E/c$.

nodes.label: Classical Wave Theory Failures
nodes.note: Wave theory predicts emission for any frequency given enough intensity and a time lag, both contradicted experimentally. Photons fix this via $$K_{max} = h\nu - \phi$$, independent of intensity.

nodes.label: Photocell I-V Curves
nodes.note: In a vacuum photocell, current rises with collector voltage then saturates: $$i_{sat} = \frac{ne}{t}$$. The stopping voltage intercept gives $h/e$.

nodes.label: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: De Broglie extended wave-particle duality to matter: $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$.

nodes.label: De Broglie Wavelength
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: Every moving particle has an associated wavelength: $$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$. Macroscopic momenta give negligibly small $\lambda$, hiding wave behavior.

nodes.label: Electron Wavelength
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: An electron at $10^6\ \text{m}/\text{s}$ has $$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} \approx 0.73\ \text{nm}$$, comparable to atomic spacings, hence diffraction.

nodes.label: Electron Accelerated Through V
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: After acceleration through potential $V$, $$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} \approx \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{nm}$$. This sets the resolving scale of electron microscopes.

nodes.label: Davisson-Germer Experiment
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: Electrons scattered off nickel showed diffraction peaks at angles matching Bragg's law: $$2d\sin\theta = n\lambda$$. It confirmed matter waves directly.

nodes.label: Matter Waves in Bohr Orbits
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: Allowed orbits fit an integer number of de Broglie wavelengths: $$2\pi r_n = n\lambda = \frac{nh}{mv}$$. This recovers Bohr's angular momentum quantization.

nodes.label: Standing Wave Check
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: For the $n=2$ orbit of hydrogen, the circumference fits exactly two de Broglie wavelengths: $$2\pi r_2 = 2\lambda, \ \lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$.

nodes.label: Atomic Structure
nodes.note: Rutherford's scattering established the nuclear atom. Bohr quantized its stationary states: $$mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$$.

nodes.label: Rutherford Scattering
nodes.note: Alpha particles deflect off a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. Distance of closest approach is $$r_{min} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{2Ze^2}{K}$$.

nodes.label: Bohr Radius and Orbit Scaling
nodes.note: $$r_n = \frac{n^2}{Z}a_0, \ a_0 = 0.529\ \text{nm}$$. Radii grow as $n^2$, so outer orbits are much larger.

nodes.label: Bohr Energy Levels
nodes.note: $$E_n = -\frac{13.6\,Z^2}{n^2}\ \text{eV}$$. The negative sign means the electron is bound; ionization is the transition to $E = 0$.

nodes.label: Rydberg Formula and Spectral Series
nodes.note: $$\frac{1}{\lambda} = RZ^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$$. Lyman ends at $n=1$ (UV), Balmer at $n=2$ (visible), Paschen at $n=3$ (IR).

nodes.label: Balmer H-alpha
nodes.note: The H-alpha line is $n=3 \to n=2$: $$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{5R}{36}, \ \lambda \approx 656\ \text{nm}$$.

nodes.label: Ionization Energy and Excitation
nodes.note: Energy to remove an electron from level $n$ is $$E_{ion} = \frac{13.6\,Z^2}{n^2}\ \text{eV}$$. Excitation energy to the next level is the difference of level energies.

nodes.label: Quantum Mechanics
nodes.note: Quantum mechanics replaces trajectories with wavefunctions. The Schrodinger equation $$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\psi + V\psi = E\psi$$ governs it.

nodes.label: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
nodes.note: Position and momentum cannot both be sharp: $$\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}$$. It forbids definite electron orbits inside the atom.

nodes.label: Uncertainty Estimate
nodes.note: If an electron is confined to a nucleus of size $\Delta x \approx 10^{-14}\ \text{m}$, then $$\Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2\Delta x} \approx 5.3 \times 10^{-21}\ \text{kg m/s}$$, implying kinetic energies of tens of MeV.

nodes.label: Born Probability Interpretation
nodes.note: $$|\psi|^2$$ is the probability density: $$P(x) = |\psi(x)|^2$$. The wavefunction itself is not directly observable.

nodes.label: Four Quantum Numbers
nodes.note: $n$ sets shell, $l$ sets subshell shape ($0 \le l \le n-1$), $m_l$ sets orientation ($-l \le m_l \le l$), and $m_s = \pm\frac{1}{2}$ sets spin.

nodes.label: Electronic Configuration Rules
nodes.note: Aufbau fills lowest energy first with the $(n+l)$ rule, Pauli allows at most two electrons per orbital, and Hund maximizes spin multiplicity: $$S = \frac{1}{2}\times(\text{unpaired electrons})$$.

nodes.label: Nitrogen Example
nodes.note: Nitrogen ($Z = 7$): $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$. Hund puts all three $2p$ electrons in separate orbitals with parallel spins, giving $S = 3/2$.

nodes.label: X-Rays and Nuclear Physics
nodes.note: X-rays probe inner-shell transitions, radioactive decay is statistical, and mass defects power nuclei: $$\Delta E = \Delta m\,c^2$$.

nodes.label: Moseley's Law
nodes.note: Characteristic X-ray frequency follows $$\sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b)$$. It reorganized the periodic table by atomic number.

nodes.label: Duane-Hunt Cutoff
nodes.note: The shortest bremsstrahlung wavelength from an X-ray tube is $$\lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}$$. Higher tube voltage shifts the cutoff to shorter wavelengths.

nodes.label: Radioactive Decay Law
nodes.note: $$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}, \ T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$. Activity is $A = \lambda N$.

nodes.label: Binding Energy
nodes.note: $$B = \left[Zm_p + (A-Z)m_n - M\right]c^2$$. Peak binding energy per nucleon near iron explains fusion and fission energy release.

nodes.label: Compton Scattering
nodes.note: X-rays scattered off electrons show a wavelength shift: $$\Delta\lambda = \frac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$$. It proved photon momentum $p = h/\lambda$.

nodes.label: Half-Life Example
nodes.note: A sample with $T_{1/2} = 3$ days drops to $$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/3}$$. After 9 days only $1/8$ remains.
